title: Randomisation, contamination and the novelty effect

videos.script: Lesson 7 said an experiment works because the split is random. This lesson is about the ways it stops being random without anybody noticing. {{intro}} First, the split itself. A visitor who sees the new page today and the old one tomorrow has been in both groups. The split has to be sticky, and it has to be checked. {{sticky}} If the groups come out fifty-one to forty-nine when they should be fifty-fifty, something is wrong with the plumbing, and no result from that test can be trusted. {{ratio}} Second, contamination. A person with a phone and a laptop can be two visitors. Two friends can tell each other about the new page. Then the control group has seen the treatment, and the difference shrinks. {{contamination}} Third, time. People notice something new and click on it because it is new. In Panela's test, the new checkout won by a point in the first week, and by almost nothing after. {{novelty}} By the end you will have checked Panela's split, measured its novelty effect, and know what to ask of any test before believing it. {{end}}
